common_name: Beni Kaze Japanese Forest Grass (Red-Tinted Fall-Color Hakonechloa)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring as new growth begins in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; growth is slow the first two seasons.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and cut the whole clump back to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. Beni Kaze (Japanese for 'red wind') is a solid-green Japanese forest grass selection valued for its exceptional fall color, when the cascading, arching foliage turns a vivid red-orange far more intense than the more muted bronze tones typical of most hakonechloa cultivars. Through the growing season it forms the same graceful, cascading mounds of bamboo-like green foliage as other forest grass selections, making it a strong textural companion to hostas, ferns, and heuchera before its fall color display takes center stage. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 4–5 years as growth increases.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring as new growth begins in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; growth is slow the first two seasons.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and cut the whole clump back to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. Albostriata bears arching, bamboo-like blades striped in crisp white over green, a slightly more vigorous and sun-tolerant variegated selection than the golden 'Aureola', with white-and-green coloring that reads as cooler and brighter in deep shade than gold-variegated cultivars. Its cascading, fountain-like habit works equally well as a woodland-edge groundcover, container specimen, or textural companion to hostas and ferns. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 4–5 years as growth increases.

common_name: Nicolas Japanese Forest Grass (Green-to-Orange Fall Color Hakonechloa)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring as new growth begins in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; growth is slow the first two seasons.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and cut the whole clump back to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. Nicolas is a solid-green Japanese forest grass selection prized for its dramatic seasonal transformation, holding rich green, cascading foliage through summer before turning striking shades of orange and copper-red in fall, a more pronounced color shift than many hakonechloa cultivars offer. Its bold fall display extends the season of interest for this slow, graceful, arching grass well past the typical late-summer peak of most shade perennials. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 4–5 years as growth increases.

common_name: Prairie Fire Carex (Orange-Red New Zealand Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color intensifies with more sun exposure.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color deepens and intensifies with more direct sun exposure. Prairie Fire is a New Zealand sedge cultivar with fine, arching foliage that shifts through warm tones of orange, copper, and red depending on season and light, a fiery color unlike the greens and blues typical of most ornamental sedges. Its low, fountain-like mound provides season-long color and texture in a rock garden, border edge, or mixed container without needing bloom to carry visual interest. Comb out dead blades by hand each spring rather than shearing, since cutting the evergreen foliage back hard can leave the clump looking ragged for weeks; divide congested clumps in spring every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Frosty Curls produces a dense, tousled mound of fine, silvery-green, thread-like blades that curl and twist at the tips, giving the whole plant a soft, frosted, almost woolly texture unlike the straighter blades of most sedges. Its pale, cool coloring and curling texture make it a distinctive accent for containers, rock gardens, and border edges where a soft, contrasting foil to bolder-leaved companions is wanted. Comb out dead blades by hand each spring to keep the evergreen foliage looking tidy, and divide congested clumps in spring every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Pewter Lace Fern (Silvery Hybrid Painted Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Pewter Lace bears finely cut, lacy fronds in a cool, metallic pewter-silver overlaid with darker gray-green tones and deep burgundy-red stems, a more finely dissected, delicate frond texture than the broader-cut leaves of many Japanese painted fern hybrids. Its refined, silvery texture provides a soft, luminous accent in a shaded border, contrasting well with the bolder leaves of hostas and heucheras nearby. Cut back old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Silver Falls Fern (Cascading Silvery Painted Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Silver Falls produces heavily silvered fronds with a soft, arching, slightly weeping habit that cascades gracefully over its own crown, deep burgundy-red stems providing strong color contrast against the pale silver-gray frond color. Its arching, flowing form suits it well to the edge of a raised bed, container, or rock garden where the cascading fronds can drape over an edge, in addition to standard use in a shaded border alongside hostas and heucheras. Cut back old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.
